title: Europe’s Tide of Citizen Assemblies: Unsung Success or Anticlimax?
gist: Richard Youngs notes citizen assemblies have become a mainstream, institutionalized feature of European democracy at every level, yet democratic malaise and far-right gains have worsened alongside them. He weighs a skeptical reading (little systemic impact; Hungary and Poland recovered via parties, protests and EU pressure) against a call for a 'second phase' tackling scaling, accountability, trade-offs, repolarization against antidemocrats, and relevance to Europe's 'get-things-done' capacity agenda.

insights.claim: Citizen assemblies have multiplied across Western and Eastern Europe at local, regional, national and EU levels, with nearly all major European cities now running some deliberative process and the European Commission holding regular pan-European citizen panels, including one on democracy.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Deliberative mechanisms are becoming a standard input to European policymaking.
insights.quote: Across Europe, nearly all major cities now have some form of deliberative process.

insights.claim: The COVID-19 pandemic and the climate crisis acted as catalysts for a dramatic rise in city-level assemblies, and permanent assemblies now exist in eastern Belgium, Paris, Brussels (mixed with politicians) and civic-led in Stavanger, Norway.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Crises accelerate institutional experimentation in governance.
insights.quote: Both the COVID-19 pandemic and the climate crisis acted as catalysts for a dramatic increase in the number of city-level assemblies.
insights.locator: Across Europe, nearly all major cities

insights.claim: Hundreds of organizations have begun using AI tools to scale citizen deliberation and more easily find consensual output.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Civic-tech is an emerging application area for AI deliberation tools.
insights.quote: hundreds of organizations have begun to use AI tools to enhance and scale up citizen deliberation
insights.locator: Civic groups are creating more assemblies

insights.claim: Skepticism toward citizen assemblies has evaporated in a decade, and they now enjoy support across the political spectrum from far left to far right.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Cross-ideological buy-in makes assemblies durable regardless of election outcomes.
insights.quote: They are supported across the political spectrum, from the far left through the center to the far right.
insights.locator: In the last decade, the skepticism

insights.claim: As citizen assemblies have spread, democracy scores have stagnated or worsened in many places and the far right has gained support in most European countries where assemblies have been numerous.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Procedural innovations are not offsetting the populist trend that drives European political risk.
insights.quote: In most European countries where assemblies have been numerous, the far right is on the march and gaining support.

insights.claim: Democratic recovery in Hungary and Poland was driven by protests, party alliances, new leadership, social media campaigns and EU pressure rather than deliberative forums.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Traditional political actors and EU leverage remain the decisive levers of democratic change.
insights.quote: Driving democratic recovery here was a combination of protests, party alliances, new leadership, social media campaigns, citizens moving into new political parties, and EU pressure.

insights.claim: Youngs flags a conflict of interest in assembly advocacy, since leading advocates are often involved in running assemblies or advising consulting firms that do so.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Claims of deliberative success should be discounted for advocate bias.
insights.quote: those leading the advocacy have generally been involved in either running assemblies or advising consulting organizations that do so—analysis and practitioner interest unhealthily overlapping

insights.claim: Youngs contrasts enthusiasm for AI in deliberation with what he calls the tech barons' destruction of basic freedom and human agency worldwide.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Reflects growing European hostility toward big tech, relevant to regulatory risk.
insights.quote: The current enthusiasm over using AI in deliberation is small matter compared with the so-called tech barons’ destruction of basic freedom and human agency worldwide.

insights.claim: Scaling assemblies from dozens to thousands will require coordination and an authority to adjudicate when assemblies clash or cut across each other.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Governance complexity rises if participatory processes gain formal decision power.
insights.quote: As their numbers increase, assemblies will begin to clash with and cut across each other, and some authority will have to adjudicate between them.
insights.locator: From Individual Forums to an Ecosystem

insights.claim: Assembly champions have paid little attention to 'negative accountability': who is responsible for correcting course when an assembly's decision goes drastically wrong after it has disbanded.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Policy made via assemblies may carry unclear accountability, raising policy-reversal risk.
insights.quote: It is striking how little attention assemblies’ champions have paid to this negative accountability.

insights.claim: If polarization keeps deepening despite thousands of assemblies, Youngs expects pressure to shift from depolarization toward a hardball 'repolarization' against antidemocrats.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: Signals potential for sharper confrontational politics against illiberal parties in Europe.
insights.quote: an increasing focus on repolarization against antidemocrats, as opposed to depolarization

insights.claim: European governments and the EU now prioritize centralized, effective capacity in economic, defense, climate and tech policy, and citizen assemblies must show they contribute to this get-things-done ethos or risk becoming marginalia.
insights.speaker: Richard Youngs
insights.so_what: European policy is tilting toward state capacity and speed in industrial, defense and tech domains.
insights.quote: The next generation of citizen assemblies will need to show that microlevel deliberative exercises can contribute to this get-things-done ethos and are not democracy’s esoteric marginalia.
